claims.text: A source of finance is any means by which a business obtains the money it needs to start up, operate or grow.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

claims.text: The legal form of ownership a business takes determines which sources of finance are legally available to it and how willing providers are to supply them.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

claims.text: A sole trader cannot issue shares, because an unincorporated business has no share capital to sell. Capital therefore comes from the owner's own resources, retained profit, borrowing, trade credit and asset finance, and a sole trader may also obtain a grant or use crowd funding where the provider's criteria allow.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

notes: Repaired 2026-09-08 under CR-003 (standard v0.2.0-draft) after the RS-28 review. RS-33: the legal impossibility is retained and labelled; the availability list is no longer closed.

claims.text: A partnership can raise capital from existing partners, from admitting new partners, from retained profit and from borrowing, but it cannot sell shares.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

claims.text: A private limited company can issue shares, but only privately to people it invites; it cannot offer shares for sale to the general public.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

claims.text: A public limited company may offer its shares for sale to the general public. This opens a source of equity that forms without publicly tradable shares do not have, and it is how the largest sums of equity capital are raised.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

notes: Repaired 2026-09-08 under CR-003 (standard v0.2.0-draft) after the RS-28 review. RS-33: "far larger than any other form of ownership" removed; the legal permission is what is universal.

claims.text: Incorporation makes the company a separate legal person, so the company itself is the borrower and it is the company's assets, cash flow and trading record that a lender assesses.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

notes: Express conditionally. The relationship is typical, not guaranteed: a large, long-established sole trader may borrow more cheaply than a new limited company (RS-21).

Repaired 2026-09-08 under CR-003 (standard v0.2.0-draft) after the RS-28 review. RS-33 + review issue 001. The original claim stated the lender-risk mechanism backwards and has been split into three: separate legal personality, what limited liability actually does, and what disclosure does.

claims.text: A social enterprise is defined by its objectives, not by a legal form: it may trade as a sole trader, partnership, company or co-operative and raises finance through whichever form it has adopted. Because its objectives include a social or environmental return, it may also qualify for grants, donations and impact investment. Eligibility is set by each provider's criteria and by what the money is for, not by the label a business gives itself.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

notes: Repaired 2026-09-08 under CR-003 (standard v0.2.0-draft) after the RS-28 review. RS-33: the open/closed framing was wrong; a profit-seeking business can also win a grant if the scheme fits.

claims.text: A franchisee often finds borrowing easier than an independent start-up because the franchisor's established trading record reduces the lender's perceived risk.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

claims.text: A co-operative raises capital mainly from its members and from borrowing; it cannot usually sell equity to outside investors without changing its character.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

claims.text: Limited liability limits what the owners can lose to the amount they have invested. It does not reduce the lender's exposure - it removes the owners' personal assets from the lender's reach - which is why a lender may ask an incorporated business for security over company assets, or for personal guarantees from its directors.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope; requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

notes: Repaired 2026-09-08 under CR-003 (standard v0.2.0-draft) after the RS-28 review. Added to correct review issue 001: the original claim had the mechanism inverted.

claims.text: Disclosure, audit and filing duties depend on the type of company and on the country. Where a company must file accounts, the published record gives a lender or investor verified information to assess, which can make finance easier to obtain; where no such duty applies, that advantage does not arise.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope; requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

notes: Repaired 2026-09-08 under CR-003 (standard v0.2.0-draft) after the RS-28 review. Added to correct review issue 001 and to satisfy RS-23: the original treated publication of audited accounts as a universal consequence of incorporation.

claims.text: An internal source of finance is money raised from within the business or from its owners, without borrowing from or selling ownership to an outside party.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

notes: Scope narrowed 2026-09-08 under CR-003 (RS-40): this claim describes the category, so it serves the container objective. Members are served by their own claims. The original listed every member, which let three shared items inherit fifteen objectives each and manufacture coverage.

claims.text: Internal sources charge no interest and dilute no ownership, and they are limited by what the business or its owners already have. They are not therefore free of cost or of outsiders: sale and leaseback needs a buyer and creates a lease payment, selling an asset gives up whatever that asset would have earned, and cash released from working capital has to be taken out of inventory, receivables or supplier terms.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

claims.text: Owner's investment is money the owner puts into the business from personal wealth.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

claims.text: Owner's investment costs no interest and does not dilute control, but it is limited by the owner's personal wealth and exposes the owner's own assets to business risk.

claims.text: Retained earnings are profits kept in the business after tax and after any dividends have been paid.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

claims.text: Retained earnings charge no interest and dilute no ownership, but they are available only to a business that has already been profitable, and only to the extent that the profit is still held as cash rather than already spent on assets, inventory or debt repayment. Using them also means smaller dividends, which shareholders may resent.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

claims.text: A start-up cannot use retained earnings, because it has not yet made a profit to retain.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

claims.text: Sale of unwanted assets converts non-current assets the business no longer needs into cash.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

claims.text: Selling unwanted assets raises cash without debt or dilution, but it is a one-off source, depends on such assets existing, and an asset sold under time pressure may fetch less than its book value.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

claims.text: Sale and leaseback means selling a non-current asset the business uses, usually to a finance company, and then leasing it back so the business continues to use it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

claims.text: Sale and leaseback releases a large sum of cash at once while the business keeps using the asset, but ownership and any future rise in the asset's value are given up, and the lease payments become a fixed cost the business must meet whatever its trading position.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

notes: Jurisdiction-sensitive. The general business principle holds internationally; the legal detail varies by country. Teach the principle and say that local law controls the detail (RS-23).

claims.text: Working capital can act as an internal source of finance when cash is released from within the operating cycle, for example by reducing inventory, collecting trade receivables sooner, or taking longer to pay trade payables.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

notes: Cross-links to 5.1.2 working capital. Keep the treatment here to its use as a source of finance; the management of working capital belongs to 5.1.2.

claims.text: Releasing cash from working capital avoids external finance altogether, but cutting inventory too far risks stock-outs and lost sales, pressing customers to pay early can damage relationships, and delaying payment to suppliers can damage the business's credit standing.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

claims.text: An external source of finance is money obtained from outside the business, either by borrowing it, by selling part-ownership, or by receiving it from another party.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

claims.text: Share capital is permanent: there is no obligation to repay it and no interest to pay, so it does not burden cash flow. In exchange, ownership and control are diluted, shareholders expect dividends, and issuing shares carries administrative and legal cost.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

claims.text: A debenture is a long-term loan certificate issued by a company, usually carrying a fixed rate of interest and a fixed redemption date.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

claims.text: Debentures raise large sums without diluting ownership, and the interest is a known, predictable cost. But the interest must be paid whether or not the company makes a profit, the sum must be repaid on the redemption date, and taking on more fixed-interest debt increases the business's exposure if trading weakens.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

claims.text: Admitting a new partner brings that person's capital into a partnership, and often their skills and contacts as well.

claims.text: A new partner supplies capital without interest or repayment. The cost is a share of future profits and a share of control, and the existing partners must be willing to accept both.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

claims.text: Venture capital is equity investment by a specialist firm in a business judged to have high growth potential but also high risk.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

claims.text: Venture capital supplies equity to businesses a bank is often unwilling to lend to, because the risk is high and there may be little to secure a loan against, and it usually brings expertise, governance and contacts with it. In exchange the investor takes a substantial equity stake, expects influence over decisions, and expects to sell that stake at a profit within a few years, which shapes the strategy the business can pursue.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

claims.text: A bank overdraft is an arrangement allowing a business to withdraw more from its current account than it holds, up to an agreed limit.

claims.text: An overdraft is flexible and quick to arrange, and interest is charged only on the amount actually used, which suits short-term gaps in cash flow. But the interest rate is high, the bank can usually demand repayment at short notice, and it is unsuitable for funding non-current assets.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

claims.text: Leasing avoids a large initial outlay, spreads the cost evenly, often includes maintenance, and makes it easier to replace equipment as it becomes obsolete. Over a full lease the total paid is usually more than the purchase price, and the business never owns the asset.

But interest is payable whether or not the business trades well, security is usually required, and the lender may attach conditions to how the business operates.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

claims.text: Debt factoring is selling trade receivables to a specialist company, the factor, which pays most of their value immediately and collects the debts itself.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

claims.text: Factoring turns money owed into cash at once and passes the work of collection to the factor, which helps a business with a long cash cycle. Whether the factor also carries the loss if a customer does not pay depends on the agreement: under non-recourse factoring the factor bears that loss and charges more for doing so, while under recourse factoring the business remains responsible. The factor keeps a percentage of each invoice, so the business receives less than it is owed, and customers dealing with a factor may read it as a sign of financial difficulty.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

notes: Repaired 2026-09-08 under CR-003 (standard v0.2.0-draft) after the RS-28 review. RS-35: the original transferred bad-debt risk unconditionally.

claims.text: Trade credit is an arrangement to receive goods or services from a supplier now and pay for them at an agreed later date.

claims.text: Trade credit is interest-free short-term finance and eases cash flow at no direct cost if payment is made on time. But early-settlement discounts are lost, paying late damages supplier relationships and the business's credit standing, and a new business with no trading record may not be offered credit at all.

claims.text: Micro-finance is the provision of small loans and related financial services to individuals and very small businesses that cannot obtain finance from mainstream banks.

claims.text: Crowd funding is raising a large number of small contributions through an online platform. It takes four broad forms: donation, where the backer receives nothing in return; reward, where the backer receives the product or another benefit; equity, where the backer receives a share of the business; and loan-based, where the money is repaid with interest.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

notes: Repaired 2026-09-08 under CR-003 (standard v0.2.0-draft) after the RS-28 review. RS-35: the original definition covered only the donation and reward models.

claims.text: What crowd funding costs depends on the form. Donation and reward campaigns give up no ownership and repay nothing, though the business must deliver whatever it promised. Equity crowd funding dilutes ownership in the same way as any share issue. Loan-based crowd funding must be repaid with interest in the same way as any borrowing. Common to the forms: the campaign must be persuasive, many fail to reach their target, platforms charge fees, and the idea becomes public before launch.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication; jurisdiction-sensitive claims additionally require human approval (RS-13, RS-23).

claims.text: A government grant is a sum provided by government, normally not repayable, to encourage activity the government wishes to see.

claims.text: A grant supplies finance with no repayment, no interest and no dilution of ownership. But grants are competitive, carry conditions on what the money is used for and often on location or employment, take time to apply for, and rarely cover the full cost of a project.

claims.text: The choice of a source of finance in a given situation is influenced by its cost, its flexibility, the owners' need to retain control, the use to which the money will be put, and the level of debt the business already carries.

claims.text: A business that already carries a high level of debt is likely to face higher interest on further borrowing, more difficulty obtaining it, and greater vulnerability if sales fall, because interest must be paid whatever the trading position.

claims.text: Selecting a source of finance means judging which available source is most appropriate for a specific business in a specific situation, and being able to say why the alternatives are less suitable.

claims.text: Borrowing may be secured or unsecured. Secured borrowing names an asset the lender can take if the business does not repay, which reduces the lender's loss if that happens and usually brings a lower rate. Unsecured borrowing names no such asset, so it is generally harder to obtain and costs more.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope; requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

notes: Repaired 2026-09-08 under CR-003 (standard v0.2.0-draft) after the RS-28 review. Added for RS-35: the subject variant register lists secured/unsecured as consequential.

claims.text: The boundary between an internal and an external source is whether a party outside the business supplies the money: internal finance comes from the business's own trading, its assets or its existing owners, while external finance comes from a lender, a new owner, a supplier or a grant-giver.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope; requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The total cost of an asset bought on hire purchase is the deposit plus every instalment. The difference between that total and the cash price is what the business pays for spreading the payments.
